prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single prize part for B042 naming Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. I hold it on the science, not on the fact that all six of us ranked it first. The discovery chain is physiological in the sense the prize was designed for: proglucagon processing, the insulinotropic active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, human incretin physiology, receptor biology and then long-acting agonists tested in large randomized trials with benefit in glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal outcomes. It is original, delimited, mature and still expanding. The round-1 exchange sharpened one point for me: the citation should name the physiology and the active form and nothing about priority or about a drug product, which keeps the credit tied to what the supplied record supports. I do not think a second part is needed. A second part would only be justified if one alternative had a narrower attribution gap than B042 and an equally clear originating discovery, and none does.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weak point and the round-1 exchange did not remove it. Knudsen designed liraglutide and semaglutide, and omitting her is a real cost that the three-name cap imposes. Habener's group has a serious claim on proglucagon and on the active peptide, and I cannot adjudicate the Mojsov and Habener priority question from the supplied record; my recollection of that history is not a verified source. If the committee concludes that Mojsov's claim cannot be defended in a written justification, my fallback is Knudsen in the third place with the citation widened to the long-acting agonists, not a two-name prize. A physiology-centred citation could also be read as slighting the engineering that made the drugs, and I accept that reading is not baseless.

responses.point: The chair asks whether the record is clear enough to name Mojsov and not Habener, and proposes keeping the citation on physiology so as not to assert a priority the committee cannot adjudicate.
responses.response: I agree with the wording approach and would go slightly further. The citation I propose says 'identification of its active form' without saying who identified it first, and the names in the credit are then justified on their separate contributions: Holst on human incretin physiology, Drucker on receptor biology and translation, Mojsov on identification and synthesis of the active peptide. That does not settle priority and I do not claim it does. It means that if the committee later learns the record favours Habener's group on the peptide itself, the citation does not have to be rewritten, only the third name reconsidered. I would not call the Habener gap closed by careful wording, and I think the minutes should say so.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius holds that a three-academic-name single achievement is coherent and needs no second part, and that a split pairing GLP-1 with CAR-T or anti-TNF would force the GLP-1 credit below three names.
responses.response: I agree and this is the main reason I have not moved to a two-part configuration. Pairing B042 with B038 or B041 would take one of the GLP-1 names away from a case that already strains the three-name cap, and the gain would be a second prize whose own attribution gaps (Eshhar for B038, a narrower pair for B041) are not smaller than the one we are trying to manage. Where I differ from your list is on B041 as a fallback: I still rank it below CAR-T and HPV vaccines because its credited pair is narrower than the lines of discovery behind it. That is a difference in ordering of alternatives, not a disagreement about the preferred prize.

responses.point: Perlmann says the strongest reservation is attribution and that a physiology-only prize can under-credit the translational step, while including Knudsen displaces a basic-science contributor.
responses.response: That is the trade-off as I see it too, and I think it is a real one. I have not moved toward Knudsen in round 2 because the discovery that made the drug class possible is the physiology and the active peptide, and the long-acting engineering was built on top of them. But I would not claim the engineering was routine. Extending the half-life of a peptide degraded within minutes was a substantial achievement. I would answer the chair's question about wording by keeping Knudsen's work visible in the minutes as the cost of the cap, and by being clear that it is the cap and the discovery framing that exclude her, not a judgement that her contribution was small.

responses.point: El-Manira asks that the tool-versus-discovery question be answered once and applied consistently to B029 and B004, and sees optogenetics as a strong second choice for originality.
responses.response: I agree the rule should be stated once. My answer is that a methodological advance qualifies when it opened a new line of biological or medical discovery that is documented, and does not qualify on tool value alone. Applied to B004, sequencing technology is the base for so much of biology that the prize is better directed at the discoveries enabled with it, and I note that my own field relies on it, which is why I would not push it. Applied to B029, the originality is high but the six-name credit and the split between channelrhodopsin function and neuronal deployment still produce an unfair trio. So under the same rule neither is the stronger second part today, and I keep B038 and B013 as my alternatives because their medical consequences are demonstrated.

responses.point: Sandberg-Rickard asks what carries B041 beyond clinical efficacy, and whether B038 carries a claim comparable to B029 once Eshhar's omission is weighed.
responses.response: On B038 I think the Eshhar omission weakens it as a second part but not as an alternative, because the chimeric-receptor concept as engineered in Sadelain's and June's work and the clinical demonstration are separable and well documented, with Rosenberg's adoptive transfer a separate line that the committee would need to decide whether to include. Its attribution gap is real but no wider than those of B029 or B015 once their omissions are counted, and it has a clear medical effect that B029 does not yet have. That is why it stays first among my alternatives. I accept your point that B041 needs a clearer statement of what the discovery is beyond efficacy, and I cannot supply one from the record.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide over the Habener group holds, which the supplied credit list does not settle and which I am judging from recollection; if it fails, Knudsen is my replacement for the third name.
Whether a physiology-focused citation under-credits the long-acting agonists to a degree the committee will find unacceptable.
Whether the tool-versus-discovery rule I have stated is the rule the other members would apply, since the committee has not agreed it explicitly.
Whether Eshhar's chimeric receptor concept and Rosenberg's adoptive transfer should be inside or outside B038, which determines how good a fallback it is.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has arisen in the discussion that bears on B042, B038 or B013. My profile records a co-authored spatial transcriptomics paper and co-authorship with Rickard Sandberg, neither involving any credited person on the shortlist. B004 (massively parallel sequencing) is a technology my own field relies on, which I disclose as methodological dependence and not a personal tie to Klenerman, Mayer or Balasubramanian, and I do not rank it as a preferred part.
